question: Compute the number of ways there are to assemble $2$ red unit cubes and $25$ white unit cubes into a $3 \times 3 \times 3$ cube such that red is visible on exactly $4$ faces of the larger cube. (Rotations and reflections are considered distinct.)

completions.text:
We wish to choose two of the 27 unit cubes to be red (the other 25 will be white) so that when the 3×3×3 “big‐cube” is assembled the red “patches” show on exactly 4 of its 6 faces. (Since rotations and reflections count as different, we are not “modding out” by symmetry.)

A key observation is that only cubes on the “surface” (that is, cubes having at least one coordinate equal to 1 or 3) can show red on a face. (The single “interior” cube, at (2,2,2), is hidden.) Moreover, every surface cube lies in one of three “types” according to how many faces it touches:
 
• A corner cube touches 3 faces.
• An edge (but not corner) cube touches 2 faces.
• A face–center cube touches 1 face.

A red cube placed in a given position “contributes” the set of faces it touches. (For example, a cube at (1,2,2) touches only the face x = 1, while one at (1,1,1) touches the three faces x = 1, y = 1, and z = 1.) When two red cubes are placed, the red “visibility” is the union of their face–sets. We want exactly 4 distinct faces to show red.

Because the only surface cubes are of the three types (corner, edge, or face–center) and a red cube in the interior would show 0 faces, both red cubes must be chosen among the 26 surface cubes. (In fact, if one red cube were interior the union would have size at most 3.) A short analysis shows that the only placements that yield a union of exactly 4 faces occur in the following four cases:

───────────────────────────── 
Case 1. One red cube is a face–center (type “1”) and the other is a corner (type “3”) with no common face.

• A face–center cube lies in the center of one face. There are 6 such cubes. (For example, (1,2,2) shows only the face x = 1; (3,2,2) shows only x = 3; etc.)
• A corner cube touches 3 faces. There are 8 corners.
• For a given face–center (say, (1,2,2) which shows x = 1) the corner must not lie on the same face. (Every face contains 4 of the 8 corners.) Thus for each face–center there are 8 – 4 = 4 allowable corners.
• Total for Case 1: 6×4 = 24.
───────────────────────────── 
Case 2. Both red cubes are edge cubes (type “2”) and their face–sets are disjoint.

• There are 12 edge cubes.
• An edge cube touches 2 faces. (For example, (2,1,1) touches the faces y = 1 and z = 1.)
• When choosing 2 distinct edge cubes, if their sets of faces are disjoint then the union has 2 + 2 = 4 faces.
• A (careful) count by “grouping” the 12 edges according to which coordinate is 2 shows that the number of unordered pairs of edges with disjoint face–sets is 30.
───────────────────────────── 
Case 3. One red cube is an edge cube (type “2”) and the other is a corner (type “3”) and they share exactly 1 face.

• There are 12 edge cubes and 8 corner cubes.
• For a given edge cube (say, one with face–set {x = 1, z = 1}) one may check that exactly 4 of the 8 corners have intersection of size 1 with {x = 1, z = 1} (namely, those that share x = 1 but not z = 1, or share z = 1 but not x = 1).
• Thus the total number in Case 3 is 12×4 = 48.
───────────────────────────── 
Case 4. Both red cubes are corners (type “3”) and they share exactly 2 faces.

• Two distinct corner cubes have face–sets of size 3. Their intersection is the set of coordinates on which they agree.
• For the union to have size 4 we need
  3 + 3 – |intersection| = 4  ⟹ |intersection| = 2.
• In other words, the two corners must agree on exactly 2 coordinates (and hence differ in the third).
• For each coordinate (3 choices) if we fix the other two (2 choices each, so 2² = 4 ways) the two differing values give one pair. Thus the number is 3×4 = 12.
───────────────────────────── 

Now, adding the counts from the four cases we get:
  24 + 30 + 48 + 12 = 114.

Thus, there are 114 ways to choose 2 red cubes (and hence assemble the 3×3×3 cube with 25 white cubes) so that red appears on exactly 4 faces.

The final answer is 114.

A key observation is that a red cube that is not on the surface does not show at all. (The only interior cube is at (2,2,2) in a natural coordinate system.) Thus, to have red visible on any face the red cubes must lie on the surface. (In fact, if one red cube were interior and the other on the surface the total number of faces showing red would be at most 3.) Hence both red cubes must be chosen from the 26 “surface‐cubes.”

On the surface a unit cube may lie in one of three “types” according to how many faces it touches:
 • A corner cube touches 3 faces.
 • An edge (noncorner) cube touches 2 faces.
 • A face–center cube touches 1 face.

In our 3×3×3 cube there are exactly 8 corners, 12 edges, and 6 face–centers (8+12+6 = 26).

Now, label the 6 faces of the big cube by
  x = 1, x = 3, y = 1, y = 3, z = 1, and z = 3.

When two red cubes are placed, the set of faces on which red is seen is the union of their individual face–sets. We require that
  |F(red cube 1) ∪ F(red cube 2)| = 4.

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. Both red cubes are corners.
──────────────────────────────
A corner cube shows 3 faces. If the two corners are “well separated” (that is, not sharing any face) their union would have 3+3 = 6 faces. In fact, if the two corners share k faces then
  |F(X) ∪ F(Y)| = 3 + 3 – k = 6 – k.
To have 6 – k = 4 we must have k = 2. (Sharing only 1 face would give 5 and sharing 0 would give 6.)
 
Now, when do two corner cubes share exactly 2 faces? They must lie on a common edge of the big cube. (Any two distinct corners on the same edge share the two faces that bound that edge.) There are 12 edges of a cube and each edge has exactly 2 corner cubes. Thus the number of unordered pairs of adjacent (edge–sharing) corners is 12.

──────────────────────────────
Case 2. One red cube is a corner and the other is an edge.
──────────────────────────────
A corner shows 3 faces and an edge (but not–corner) cube shows 2 faces. In general the union has size
  3 + 2 – |F(corner) ∩ F(edge)|.
To get a union of 4 we need
  5 – |F(corner) ∩ F(edge)| = 4  ⟹ |F(corner) ∩ F(edge)| = 1.
That is, the corner and the edge must share exactly one face.

Since there are 8 corners, the total number of unordered pairs (corner, edge) with the desired property is 8×6 = 48.

──────────────────────────────
Case 3. Both red cubes are edge cubes.
──────────────────────────────
An edge cube shows 2 faces. If two edge cubes have face–sets F and G then
  |F ∪ G| = 2 + 2 – |F ∩ G|.
To have |F ∪ G| = 4 we must have |F ∩ G| = 0; that is, the two edge cubes must show no common face.

──────────────────────────────
Case 4. One red cube is a face–center and the other is a corner.
──────────────────────────────
A face–center cube shows 1 face and a corner shows 3 faces. Their union has size
  1 + 3 – |F(face–center) ∩ F(corner)|.
For the union to have 4 faces we need
  4 – |F(face–center) ∩ F(corner)| = 4  ⟹ |F(face–center) ∩ F(corner)| = 0.
That is, the unique face on which the face–center lies must not be one of the 3 faces of the corner.
 
For example, if the face–center is on the face x = 1 (say at (2,2,1)) then its only visible face is “x = 1”. To have no common face the corner must not lie on x = 1 – that is, its x–coordinate must be 3. There are 4 corners with x = 3. By symmetry the same count holds for a face–center on any face. Since there are 6 face–centers, the total number of unordered pairs (face–center, corner) with no common face is 6×4 = 24.

──────────────────────────────
Other Possibilities
──────────────────────────────
One might also consider a pair consisting of a face–center and an edge cube or two face–centers. However, a face–center shows only 1 face and an edge shows 2 faces so their union can have at most 3 faces; and two face–centers show at most 2 faces. Thus no other type of pair can yield exactly 4 red faces.

──────────────────────────────
Adding Up the Cases
──────────────────────────────
Now we add the counts from the four cases:
 
 Case 1 (corner–corner): 12
 Case 2 (corner–edge):  48
 Case 3 (edge–edge):   30
 Case 4 (face–center–corner): 24
 
Total = 12 + 48 + 30 + 24 = 114.

──────────────────────────────
Answer
──────────────────────────────
There are 114 ways to choose two red unit cubes (from the 27 positions) so that when the 3×3×3 cube is assembled exactly 4 of its faces show red.

Thus, the answer is 114.

• A “corner” red cube (one of the 8 cubes at a vertex) touches exactly 3 faces.

Since we want red to be seen on exactly 4 faces overall, and since a single red cube can contribute at most 3 faces, both red cubes must lie on the surface. (For example, if one were interior its contribution would be 0 and the other at most 3, giving at most 3 visible red faces.)

Step 1. Classify the 26 surface positions by type:
 
  • Type A (“face–center”): 6 positions. Each such cube touches 1 face.
  • Type B (“edge”): 12 positions. Each such cube touches 2 faces.
  • Type C (“corner”): 8 positions. Each such cube touches 3 faces.

A Type A cube touches a single face. There are 6 such positions. For a given Type A cube (say it touches face f), a Type C (corner) cube touches 3 faces. Now one red cube is on an edge (Type B, 2 faces) and the other is at a corner (Type C, 3 faces). For a fixed Type B cube (say with face–set {f, g}), we want to count how many Type C cubes have exactly one of f and g among their 3 faces.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

Both red cubes are at corners. A corner cube touches 3 faces. For two distinct corner cubes the number of common faces equals the number of coordinates in which they agree.   Case I: 24

  Case III: 48 
  Case IV: 12 
  Total = 24 + 30 + 48 + 12 = 114.

We wish to build a 3×3×3 cube from 27 unit cubes – 2 red and 25 white – so that when the large cube is “assembled” the red shows on exactly 4 of its 6 faces. (Here “red is visible on a face” means that at least one red unit cube lies in a position on that face.) In our count rotations and reflections count as different, so we are simply “choosing” which two of the 27 positions get the red cubes subject to the extra condition.

A key observation is that a red cube that is not on the surface does not contribute any red to any face. (There is exactly one interior cube in a 3×3×3, and it touches no face.) Also, a red cube on the surface may “cover” more than one face. (For example, a red cube at a corner shows on 3 faces.) Thus, to have red on 4 faces the two red cubes must both lie on the surface and “together” their set of incident faces (i.e. the union of the faces on which they lie) must have exactly 4 elements.

Let’s first classify the 27 positions by “type” (only surface positions matter here):

• Corners: 8 positions. Each corner touches 3 faces.
• Edges (but not corners): 12 positions. Each such “edge‐cube” touches 2 faces.
• Face–centers: 6 positions. Each touches 1 face.
• Interior: 1 position (touches 0 faces).

Since an interior red would contribute 0 faces and a single surface cube contributes at most 3 faces, both red cubes must be chosen from the surface. Moreover, if the two red cubes are on the surface, then the set of faces that are “red‐visible” is the union of the sets of faces on which each red cube lies. (For example, a corner gives a set of 3 faces, an edge gives 2, and a face–center gives 1.) We now break the counting into cases according to the “types” of the two red cubes. In every case the union (set) of faces from the two cubes must have exactly 4 elements.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. (Corner, Corner)

A corner cube “covers” 3 faces. If we have two corners with face–sets A and B then
  |A ∪ B| = 3 + 3 – |A ∩ B| = 6 – |A ∩ B|.
We need 6 – |A ∩ B| = 4, so |A ∩ B| must equal 2.

When do two distinct corner cubes share exactly 2 faces? They share 2 faces precisely when they lie on the same edge of the big cube (since two corners on a common edge have the same two “side” faces). (They cannot share all 3 because that would force them to be the same cube.) 

Now, every edge of the cube has exactly 2 corner cubes. Since a cube has 12 edges, there are exactly 12 pairs of corners that lie on the same edge. 

Thus, the number of (corner,corner) placements is 12.
───────────────────────────── 
Step 2. (Corner, Edge)

A corner cube covers 3 faces and an edge cube covers 2 faces. If the corner’s face–set is A and the edge’s is B then
  |A ∪ B| = 3 + 2 – |A ∩ B| = 5 – |A ∩ B|.
We require 5 – |A ∩ B| = 4 so that |A ∩ B| = 1.

How can a corner and an edge share exactly 1 face? (Remember: a face is determined by a coordinate being 1 or 3.) A corner, say at (1,1,1) (using coordinates in {1,2,3} where the outer layer is given by 1 or 3) touches the faces x=1, y=1, and z=1. An edge cube has exactly two coordinates equal to 1 or 3 (and the remaining coordinate equal to 2). For the two cubes to share exactly one face, exactly one of the two “boundary‐coordinates” of the edge cube must equal the corresponding coordinate of the corner.

A short check (by listing the 12 edge positions relative to the corner (1,1,1)) shows that exactly 6 of the 12 edge cubes have exactly one coordinate equal to 1 (matching the corner’s coordinate) while the other coordinate (of the two on the boundary) is different. By symmetry the answer is the same for any corner.

Since there are 8 corners and for each corner there are 6 valid edge cubes, the total number in this case is 8×6 = 48.
───────────────────────────── 
Step 3. (Corner, Face–center)

A corner gives 3 faces and a face–center gives 1 face. Their union has size
  3 + 1 – |A ∩ B| = 4 – |A ∩ B|.
To have union = 4 we must have |A ∩ B| = 0; that is, the face–center must lie on a face that the corner does not touch.

A given corner (say at (1,1,1)) touches the three faces x=1, y=1, and z=1. The other 3 faces of the cube (namely x=3, y=3, and z=3) are not touched by that corner. And on each face there is exactly 1 face–center. Thus for any corner there are 3 valid face–centers.

With 8 corners, the total number here is 8×3 = 24.
───────────────────────────── 
Step 4. (Edge, Edge)

Each edge cube covers 2 faces. For two edge cubes with face–sets A and B we have
  |A ∪ B| = 2 + 2 – |A ∩ B| = 4 – |A ∩ B|.
We need this to equal 4 so that |A ∩ B| = 0; that is, the two edge cubes must not share any face.

How can two edge cubes share a face? Two edge cubes lie on a common face if they are among the 4 edge cubes on that face. (Each face of the big cube has 4 edges.) Thus, for a given face there are C(4,2) = 6 pairs of edge cubes that share that face. Since there are 6 faces, one might “naively” count 6×6 = 36 pairs that share a face. (Note that any two distinct edge cubes share at most one face.)

There are a total of C(12,2) = 66 pairs of edge cubes. Subtracting the 36 pairs that share a face leaves 66 – 36 = 30 pairs with no common face.

Thus, the number in this case is 30.
───────────────────────────── 
Step 5. (Edge, Face–center) and (Face–center, Face–center)

A red cube on a face–center covers only 1 face. In an (edge, face–center) pair the maximum union is 2+1 = 3 (if they share no face) or even less if they do share a face. Thus it is impossible for an (edge, face–center) pair to cover 4 faces. Similarly, two face–centers cover at most 2 faces. So no placements occur in these types.

───────────────────────────── 
Final Count

Now add the counts from the four valid cases:
  Corner–Corner: 12 
  Corner–Edge:  48 
  Corner–Face–center: 24 
  Edge–Edge:   30 
Total = 12 + 48 + 24 + 30 = 114.

───────────────────────────── 
Answer

There are 114 ways to choose positions for the 2 red cubes (with the remaining 25 white) so that exactly 4 faces of the 3×3×3 cube show red.

We will show that when two of the 27 unit cubes are painted red and the other 25 are white, the only placements that yield “exactly 4 red faces visible” (when the 3×3×3 cube is assembled) occur when both red cubes lie on the surface and, more precisely, when the two red cubes “cover” exactly 4 different faces of the big cube. In what follows “visible” means that the red unit cube lies in a position on the boundary of the 3×3×3 so that one of its faces is on the exterior.

In our 3×3×3 cube the 27 positions break into types according to how many faces they touch:
 • 8 corner cubes (each touches 3 faces),
 • 12 edge cubes (each touches 2 faces),
 • 6 face‐center cubes (each touches 1 face),
 • 1 interior cube (touches 0 faces).

A red cube that is not on the surface would not show red on any face. (In fact, if one red cube were interior the only red visible would come from the other red cube – at most 3 faces if that cube is a corner.) Hence both red cubes must be chosen from the 26 surface cubes.

Now, if a red cube is placed in a given surface position its “red–face set” is the set of the big–cube faces that it touches. (For example, a cube at (1,1,1) touches the faces x=1, y=1, and z=1.) When two red cubes are placed the union of their red–face sets is exactly the set of faces that show red. We want this union to have exactly 4 elements.

A short calculation shows that if a cube touches f faces and another touches g faces then for their union to have 4 faces we must have

  f + g – |intersection| = 4.

Since the only possibilities on the surface are f = 3, 2, or 1, one may check that the only cases that can work are:

1. Two corner cubes (f = 3 each) must share exactly 2 faces. (Because 3+3–|intersection| = 6–|intersection| = 4 forces |intersection| = 2.)  
2. A corner (3 faces) together with an edge (2 faces) must share exactly 1 face.  
3. A corner (3 faces) together with a face–center (1 face) must have no common face.  
4. Two edge cubes (2 faces each) must have no common face.

Any other pairing would give a union of size 1, 2, 3, 5, or 6.

We now count the number of unordered pairs {p,q} (with p and q chosen from the 26 surface cubes) in each case.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Case 1. Two corner cubes sharing exactly 2 faces

Any two distinct corner cubes lie on a common edge exactly when they are “adjacent” along that edge. (For example, the corners (1,1,1) and (1,1,3) share the faces y=1 and z=1.) Since the 3×3×3 has 12 edges and each edge has exactly 2 corners, there are

  12 pairs

in this case.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Case 2. A corner and an edge cube sharing exactly 1 face

Label a corner cube p (for example, p = (1,1,1) has red–face set {x=1, y=1, z=1}). An edge cube q is one with exactly two coordinates equal to 1 or 3 and the third equal to 2. One may show that for a given corner p the requirement that p and q share exactly one face forces the following: if p = (a,b,c) with each a, b, c equal to 1 or 3, then q (which has two “boundary” coordinates) must have one of its boundary coordinates equal to the same value as p and the other equal to the opposite boundary value. (For instance, with p = (1,1,1) an acceptable q is (1,3,2) because its “boundary” coordinates are x = 1 and y = 3; note that (1,3,2) has face set {x=1, y=3} and its intersection with {x=1, y=1, z=1} is {x=1}.) A short check shows that for each corner there are exactly 6 edge cubes q with this property. Since there are 8 corners, the total number in this case is

  8 × 6 = 48.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Case 3. A corner and a face–center cube with no common face

A face–center cube lies in the middle of one face (so it has one coordinate equal to 1 or 3 and the other two equal to 2). For a corner p = (a,b,c) the only way for a face–center r (with, say, its unique boundary coordinate in the x–direction) to have no face in common with p is that r’s x–value is the opposite of p’s x–value. (For example, if p = (1,1,1) then a face–center on the x–face must be (3,2,2) rather than (1,2,2).) Since p has 3 coordinates and for each coordinate there is exactly 1 “opposite” value, each corner p has exactly 3 valid face–center partners. With 8 corners this gives

  8 × 3 = 24.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Case 4. Two edge cubes with no common face

An edge cube touches 2 faces. Label an edge cube by the two coordinates in which it is “on the boundary.” (For example, (2,1,1) has its y– and z–coordinates on the boundary.) One may show by a short case–analysis (or by an “coordinate–counting” argument) that if p and q are two edge cubes then in order for their red–face sets to have empty intersection the following must happen: if p’s two boundary coordinates are, say, i and j and q’s are k and ℓ, then if {i,j} and {k,ℓ} have a common element (and they always do if the two 2–element sets are different) the common coordinate must have p and q taking opposite boundary values. A careful count (which you may verify by listing the 12 edge cubes in three groups according to which coordinate equals 2) shows that among the 12 edge cubes the number of unordered pairs with no common face is

  30.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Adding the four cases we obtain a total of

  12 + 48 + 24 + 30 = 114

ways to choose two surface positions for the red cubes so that exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the big cube show red.

Therefore, if one red cube were placed in the interior it would not contribute any red “face‐visibility” and the other red cube (even if placed at a corner, where it shows on 3 faces) would yield at most 3 visible red faces. Thus both red cubes must be placed on the surface.

Step 1. Classify the Surface Cubes

In a 3×3×3 cube the 27 cubes break into:
• Corner cubes (touch 3 faces): There are 8.
• Edge cubes (but not corners; touch 2 faces): There are 12.
• Face–center cubes (touch 1 face): There are 6.
(Notice 8+12+6 = 26, which is the total number of cubes on the surface.)

For a cube in a given position the “set of faces” on which it appears is determined by its location:
– A corner cube appears on 3 faces.
– An edge cube appears on 2 faces.
– A face–center appears on 1 face.

Step 2. Understand the “Union‐of–Faces” Condition

When two red cubes are placed (in distinct positions) their combined “red–visible” faces is the union of the sets of faces on which they lie. (Even if two red cubes lie on the same face, that face is counted only once.) We require that exactly 4 different faces of the large cube show red.

If a red cube in position A shows on |S| faces and one in position B shows on |T| faces, then the total number of red faces is

  |S ∪ T| = |S| + |T| – |S ∩ T|.

Since the types have fixed sizes (corner = 3, edge = 2, face–center = 1), we now consider the possible pairs of types (A,B) and determine for which choices we can have |S ∪ T| = 4.

Step 3. Case–by–Case Analysis

There are four non–overlapping cases (we do not consider a red cube in the interior because that would not help achieve 4 visible faces):

───────────────────────────── 
Case 1. Both red cubes are placed at corners.
───────────────────────────── 
Each corner shows on 3 faces. If the two corners have sets S and T then
  |S ∪ T| = 3 + 3 – |S ∩ T| = 6 – |S ∩ T|.
To have 6 – |S ∩ T| = 4 we must have |S ∩ T| = 2.
When do two distinct corner cubes share exactly 2 faces? They must be “neighbors” along an edge of the big cube (that is, they differ in exactly one coordinate). For example, the corner at (1,1,1) and the corner at (1,1,3) share the faces x = 1 and y = 1.
A quick count shows that each corner has exactly 3 neighbors (differing in exactly one coordinate) and since the 8 corners form 12 distinct edges, there are 12 unordered pairs.
 
───────────────────────────── 
Case 2. One red cube is at a corner and the other is at an edge.
───────────────────────────── 
A corner shows on 3 faces and an edge shows on 2 faces. Their union is
  3 + 2 – |S ∩ T| = 5 – |S ∩ T|.
We need 5 – |S ∩ T| = 4, so |S ∩ T| must equal 1.
How can a corner and an edge share exactly one face? A corner touches 3 faces. On any one of those faces the big cube has 4 edge–cubes (the ones in the middle of the edge of that face). However, two of these edge–cubes are “adjacent” to the corner (they lie along the two edges emanating from that corner on that face) and would share 2 faces with the corner. Thus on each face the corner “allows” 4 – 2 = 2 choices for an edge–cube that meets the condition.
Since the corner touches 3 faces, for a given corner there are 3×2 = 6 valid edge–cubes.
With 8 corners this gives 8×6 = 48 unordered pairs.

───────────────────────────── 
Case 3. Both red cubes are placed at edge positions.
───────────────────────────── 
Each edge cube shows on 2 faces. For two edge cubes with face–sets S and T we have
  |S ∪ T| = 2 + 2 – |S ∩ T| = 4 – |S ∩ T|.
To get 4 we need |S ∩ T| = 0; that is, the two edge cubes must not share any face.
There are 12 edge cubes in all. The total number of unordered pairs among them is C(12,2) = 66.
Now, count those pairs that do share a face. (An edge cube lies on exactly 2 faces. For a given face of the big cube, there are 4 edge cubes on that face – one in the middle of each edge of that face. Thus on any given face there are C(4,2) = 6 pairs that share that face. Since the big cube has 6 faces, a first count gives 6×6 = 36. Moreover, any two distinct edge cubes cannot share two faces – so each pair is counted exactly once.)
Thus the number of edge–cube pairs with disjoint face–sets is 66 – 36 = 30.
 
───────────────────────────── 
Case 4. One red cube is at a corner and the other is at a face–center.
───────────────────────────── 
A corner shows on 3 faces and a face–center shows on 1 face. Their union is
  3 + 1 – |S ∩ T| = 4 – |S ∩ T|.
To have 4 we need |S ∩ T| = 0; that is, the face on which the face–center lies must not be one of the 3 faces touched by the corner.
Since there are 6 face–centers in all and a given corner touches 3 of them, for each corner there are 6 – 3 = 3 valid face–centers.
With 8 corners this gives 8×3 = 24 unordered pairs.
 
───────────────────────────── 
Cases Involving Two Face–Centers or an Edge and a Face–Center:
───────────────────────────── 
A face–center shows on only 1 face and an edge shows on 2 faces. Their union would be at most 3 (if they did not share a face) or less if they did share a face. Thus no pair of an edge cube with a face–center (or two face–centers) can yield a union of 4 faces.

Step 4. Add the Cases

Now, summing the valid unordered pairs from the four cases we have:
  Case 1: 12
  Case 2: 48
  Case 3: 30
  Case 4: 24
Total = 12 + 48 + 30 + 24 = 114.

Thus, there are 114 ways to choose positions for the 2 red cubes (among the 27 positions) so that exactly 4 faces of the 3×3×3 cube show red.

We wish to choose two of the 27 unit‐cube positions to be red (with the other 25 white) so that when the 3×3×3 cube is assembled the “red” appears on exactly 4 of its 6 faces. (By “red is visible on a face” we mean that at least one red unit cube lies in a position that touches that exterior face.) (Also, note that rotations and reflections count as different assemblies.)

A key observation is that a red cube contributes to a face only if it lies on the surface. (The single interior cube, at (2,2,2), touches no face.) Hence, in order for red to be seen on 4 faces the two red cubes must both lie on the surface. (If one were interior its “contribution” would be 0, and even a surface cube shows on at most 3 faces.) 

It is very useful to classify the 27 positions by how many faces they touch. In a 3×3×3 cube the positions break into four types:

• Corners (3 faces): There are 8.
• Edges (but not corners) (2 faces): There are 12.
• Face‐centers (1 face): There are 6.
• Interior (0 faces): There is 1.

Since a red cube placed in a given position “shows” on the set of faces corresponding to the coordinates equal to 1 or 3, we record for each type the number of faces that cube touches. (For example, a corner at (1,1,1) shows on the faces x = 1, y = 1, and z = 1.)

Now, if we place two red cubes in positions P and Q with “face–sets” F(P) and F(Q) (i.e. the sets of faces on which they lie), then the red is seen on the union F(P) ∪ F(Q). We require that
  |F(P) ∪ F(Q)| = 4.

Because the red cubes are identical (so order does not matter) we must count unordered pairs of surface positions (from the 8+12+6 = 26 surface cubes) for which the union of their face–sets has exactly 4 elements.

A natural approach is to break the count into cases according to the “types” of the two chosen positions. (We will not consider any pair involving the interior cube since that cube shows on 0 faces.)

Let’s denote by “corner”, “edge”, and “face–center” the three types (with the numbers in parentheses giving the number of faces each shows).

Recall:
 • A corner shows on 3 faces.
 • An edge shows on 2 faces.
 • A face–center shows on 1 face.

When two cubes are placed, if one shows on a set A and the other on a set B, then
  |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| – |A ∩ B|.
We want this union to have 4 elements.

We now consider the possible type–pairs.

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. Both cubes are corners.
──────────────────────────────
Each corner shows 3 faces. For two corners the union has size
  3 + 3 – |intersection|.
To get 4 we need
  6 – |intersection| = 4 ⟹ |intersection| = 2.
Two distinct corner cubes share exactly 2 faces precisely when they are “adjacent” along an edge of the big cube. (For example, the corners (1,1,1) and (1,3,1) share the faces x = 1 and z = 1.) 

Each edge of the cube has exactly 2 corner cubes. Since the 3×3×3 cube has 12 edges, there are 12 pairs of adjacent corners.

Thus the number of (corner, corner) pairs is 12.

──────────────────────────────
Case 2. One cube is a corner and the other is an edge.
──────────────────────────────
A corner shows on 3 faces and an edge on 2 faces. Their union has size
  3 + 2 – |intersection| = 5 – |intersection|.
We need 5 – |intersection| = 4, so |intersection| must be 1.

Thus we must choose a corner and an edge cube so that the set of faces on which they lie intersect in exactly 1 face.

A little thought shows that if you fix a given corner (say, (1,1,1) with faces {x = 1, y = 1, z = 1}), then an edge cube is determined by choosing one coordinate to be 2 (the “non–surface” value) and letting the other two coordinates be 1 or 3. (There are 3×4 = 12 edge cubes in all.) However, the three edge cubes that have the same two coordinates as the corner (for example, (2,1,1), (1,2,1), (1,1,2)) are “adjacent” to the corner and share 2 faces. A short check shows that for a given corner exactly 6 of the 12 edge cubes yield an intersection of size 1 with that corner.

Since there are 8 corners, the total number of (corner, edge) pairs is
  8 × 6 = 48.

──────────────────────────────
Case 3. One cube is a corner and the other is a face–center.
──────────────────────────────
A corner shows on 3 faces and a face–center on 1 face. Their union has size
  3 + 1 – |intersection|.
For the union to have 4 elements we need
  4 – |intersection| = 4 ⟹ |intersection| = 0.
That is, the corner and the face–center must not share any face.

Now, a given face–center lies in exactly one face. A given corner (which lies on 3 faces) will share that face with the 4 corners on that face. (For example, the face–center (1,2,2) lies on the face x = 1, and the four corners on that face are (1,1,1), (1,1,3), (1,3,1), and (1,3,3).) Thus for a given face–center there are 4 corners that share its face. Since there are 8 corners in all, for each face–center there are 8 – 4 = 4 corners that do not share its face.

With 6 face–centers, the total number of (corner, face–center) pairs is
  6 × 4 = 24.

──────────────────────────────
Case 4. Both cubes are edges.
──────────────────────────────
Each edge cube shows on 2 faces. For two edge cubes the union has size
  2 + 2 – |intersection| = 4 – |intersection|.
We need 4 – |intersection| = 4, so |intersection| must be 0. In other words, the two edge cubes must lie on no common face.

It is convenient to note that every edge of the big cube is determined by a pair of faces. (For example, the edge with positions having x = 1 and y = 1 is uniquely determined by the faces x = 1 and y = 1.) There are 12 edges in all. Two distinct edges share a face if and only if the corresponding pairs of faces have a common element. (For instance, the edges corresponding to (x = 1, y = 1) and (x = 1, z = 1) share the face x = 1.)

One may show by a short counting argument that among the C(12, 2) = 66 pairs of edges, exactly 36 pairs share a face. (For example, each face of the cube is a square and has 4 edges on its boundary; any 2 of these 4 edges share that face, and there are C(4,2) = 6 pairs per face. With 6 faces this gives 6×6 = 36 pairs. Note that no pair is counted twice because two distinct edges cannot share two faces.) 

Thus the number of pairs of edges with no common face is
  66 – 36 = 30.

──────────────────────────────
Other type–pairs
──────────────────────────────
One may check that if one or both of the red cubes is a face–center then the union of the face–sets cannot be 4 (for example, two face–centers would show on 1 + 1 – |intersection| faces, which is at most 2).

Also, if one red cube were interior (showing on 0 faces) then even with a surface cube the union would have at most 3 faces.

──────────────────────────────
Adding Up the Cases
──────────────────────────────
The total number of unordered pairs of surface positions (for the two red cubes) that yield exactly 4 visible red faces is the sum from the four cases above:
  Corner–corner: 12
  Corner–edge:  48
  Corner–face–center: 24
  Edge–edge:   30
Total = 12 + 48 + 24 + 30 = 114.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion
──────────────────────────────
There are 114 ways to choose two of the 27 positions (with both chosen on the surface) so that the red cubes appear on exactly 4 faces of the assembled 3×3×3 cube.

Thus, the answer is 114.

We wish to choose 2 of the 27 unit cubes to be red (with the other 25 white) so that when the 3×3×3 cube is assembled the red “appears” (i.e. is on the exterior) on exactly 4 of its 6 faces. (Since rotations and reflections count as different, we are not “modding out” by symmetry.)

A key observation is that a red cube placed in an interior position (the single center cube) does not show on any face. Thus, if one red cube were interior the only red “visibility” would come from the other red cube – and that cube, being on the surface, shows on at most 3 faces. (A corner shows on 3 faces, an edge on 2, and a face‐center on 1.) Hence both red cubes must lie on the surface. (There are 26 surface cubes: 8 corners, 12 edges, and 6 face–centers.)

On the surface a cube’s “visibility” is determined by which of the 6 faces it touches. In fact:
 • A corner cube touches 3 faces.
 • An edge cube touches 2 faces.
 • A face–center touches 1 face.

When we place 2 red cubes the set of faces on which red appears is the union of the faces touched by the two cubes. We require that exactly 4 distinct faces show red.

It turns out that the only placements that can yield a union of 4 faces occur in the following three cases. (We will explain each in turn.)

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. Both red cubes are placed in corners.

A corner touches 3 faces. If two corners are “adjacent” (that is, they share an edge) then they have 2 faces in common and the union of their faces is 3+3–2 = 4. (If they are not adjacent the union would have 5 or even 6 faces.) 

How many pairs of adjacent corners are there? Notice that every edge of the big cube has exactly 2 endpoints (both corners) and each such edge gives one adjacent pair. Since a cube has 12 edges, there are 12 pairs of adjacent corners.

──────────────────────────────
Case 2. Both red cubes are placed on edges.

An edge cube touches 2 faces. For two edges the union of their faces has size 2+2 minus the number of faces they share. In order for the union to have 4 faces the two edges must share no common face (since 2+2–0 = 4). 

How many pairs of edges have disjoint face–sets? There are 12 edge cubes in all. One way to count is as follows. First, note that any given face of the big cube is a 3×3 square and contains 4 edge cubes. Thus on a given face there are C(4,2) = 6 pairs of edges that share that face. Since there are 6 faces, one might “naively” count 6×6 = 36 pairs that share a face. But every pair of edges that share a face is counted once per common face (and two different edges cannot share two faces). Therefore the total number of pairs of edges that share at least one face is 36. Since the total number of unordered pairs among 12 edges is C(12,2) = 66, the number of pairs with no common face is 66 – 36 = 30.

──────────────────────────────
Case 3. One red cube is on a corner and the other is on a face–center.

A corner touches 3 faces and a face–center touches 1 face. Their union has size 3+1 minus the number of faces they share. In order for the union to be 4 the two cubes must share exactly 0 faces (since 3+1–0 = 4). 

For a given corner the three faces it touches are “claimed” by that corner. The 6 face–centers lie one per face. In order that the face–center’s face is not one of the 3 the corner touches, it must lie on one of the 3 “opposite” faces. Thus for each corner there are 3 choices for a face–center that yields a union of 4 faces. Since there are 8 corners, this gives 8×3 = 24 pairs.

──────────────────────────────
No other placements work. (For example, two face–centers would yield at most 2 faces showing red, and a corner paired with an edge that does not share a face would yield 3+2 = 5 faces.)

──────────────────────────────
Now, adding the counts from the three cases we have:
 Case 1: 12
 Case 2: 30
 Case 3: 24

Total = 12 + 30 + 24 = 66.

Thus, there are 66 ways to choose the positions for the 2 red cubes (with the remaining 25 white) so that exactly 4 faces of the large cube show red.

The final answer is 66.

We will show that when two red unit cubes (and 25 white ones) are placed in the 27 “slots” of a 3×3×3 cube, the number of placements for which exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the big cube show red is 114. (In our count the red cubes are “labeled” only by color so that two placements that differ by a rotation or reflection are counted separately.)

In what follows we describe one way to arrive at 114.

──────────────────────────────
A. The “Big‐Picture”

A 3×3×3 cube has 27 unit cubes. Exactly 26 of these lie on the surface (so that some of their faces are “visible”) while the single center cube is hidden from view. (Any red cube that is not on the surface contributes no red to any face.) Since we want red to appear on exactly 4 of the 6 faces, at least one red cube must be on the surface. In fact, if one red cube were hidden (the center) then at most the other red cube (which, being on the surface, can show on at most 3 faces) would contribute red – too few. Thus both red cubes must be placed in surface positions.

Now, on the surface a unit cube may lie in one of three “types” according to how many faces it touches:
 • A corner cube touches 3 faces.
 • An edge (but not corner) cube touches 2 faces.
 • A face‐center cube touches 1 face.
A quick count shows there are 8 corners, 12 edges, and 6 face–centers (8+12+6 = 26).

When a red cube is placed in a given surface position its “contribution” is the set of faces on which it lies. (For example, a corner at (1,1,1) “shows” the faces x = 1, y = 1, and z = 1.) If the two red cubes are in positions A and B with face–sets F(A) and F(B) then the red is visible on the faces in the union F(A) ∪ F(B). We want
  |F(A) ∪ F(B)| = 4.
Since the sizes of F(A) and F(B) depend on the type (3 for a corner, 2 for an edge, 1 for a face–center) the only possibilities (by the formula |F(A) ∪ F(B)| = |F(A)| + |F(B)| – |F(A) ∩ F(B)|) are as follows:

1. Both cubes are corners (3 + 3 – intersection = 4) ⟹ intersection must have size 2.
2. One is a corner (3) and the other an edge (2) ⟹ 3 + 2 – intersection = 4 ⟹ intersection = 1.
3. One is a corner (3) and the other a face–center (1) ⟹ 3 + 1 – intersection = 4 ⟹ intersection = 0.
4. Both cubes are edges (2 + 2 – intersection = 4) ⟹ intersection = 0.
5. The other mixed types (edge with face–center or face–center with face–center) cannot give a union of 4 (their union would be at most 3).

Thus the only cases to consider are:
  (a) Two corners with intersection = 2.
  (b) A corner and an edge with intersection = 1.
  (c) A corner and a face–center with intersection = 0.
  (d) Two edges with intersection = 0.

We now count the number of unordered pairs (that is, choices of two distinct positions among the 26 surface cubes) in each case.

──────────────────────────────
B. Case–by–Case Counting

1. Two Corners (Type “corner–corner”)

A corner cube has 3 faces. Two distinct corners will share 3 faces only if they are the same cube. (They cannot share all 3 and still be distinct.) In fact, two different corner cubes share exactly 2 faces precisely when they lie on a common edge of the big cube. (For example, the cubes at (1,1,1) and (1,1,3) share the faces y = 1 and z = 3.) 

Since the 3×3×3 cube has 12 edges and each edge has 2 corner cubes, there are exactly 12 pairs of corners that share an edge. (Each such pair gives F(A) ∪ F(B) of size 3+3–2 = 4.)

Count from this case: 12.

2. One Corner and One Edge (“corner–edge”)

Let the corner be at (i, j, k) with each coordinate 1 or 3 so that its face–set is {the face corresponding to i, to j, to k}. An edge cube is one with exactly one coordinate equal to 2 and the other two equal to 1 or 3. (There are 12 edge cubes in all.) For a given corner the intersection F(corner) ∩ F(edge) is determined by comparing the two “non–2” coordinates of the edge cube with the corner’s coordinates. A short check (for example, taking the corner (1,1,1)) shows that exactly 6 of the 12 edge cubes yield an intersection of size 1. (For instance, with the corner (1,1,1): the edge cube (2,1,3) has face–set {y = 1, z = 3} so that the intersection is {y = 1}.) By symmetry the same count holds for every corner.

Thus for each of the 8 corners there are 6 compatible edge positions. (In an unordered pair the “corner” is uniquely determined as the one of type corner.) 

Count from this case: 8×6 = 48.

3. One Corner and One Face–Center (“corner–face–center”)

A face–center cube lies in the center of one face and so has face–set of size 1. For a given corner (with face–set of size 3) an adjacent face–center (that is, one lying in one of the three faces that meet at the corner) would share that one face; we need no common face. Since there are 6 face–centers in all and exactly 3 of them lie in the three faces touched by the corner, the remaining 3 (on the opposite faces) yield an empty intersection.

Thus for each corner there are 3 compatible face–center positions.

Count from this case: 8×3 = 24.

4. Two Edges (“edge–edge”)

An edge cube has face–set of size 2. For two edge cubes the union size is 2+2 – |intersection|. To get a union of 4 we must have |intersection| = 0; that is, the two edge cubes must lie on no common face.

One way to count these is to first list the 12 edge cubes by grouping them according to which coordinate is 2. (For example, if x = 2 then the cube is of the form (2, a, b) with a,b ∈ {1,3}.) A short analysis shows that in each group of 4 the only two pairs with disjoint face–sets are the ones “opposite” in that group. (For instance, among the four cubes with x = 2 the cubes (2,1,1) with face–set {y = 1, z = 1} and (2,3,3) with {y = 3, z = 3} are disjoint; similarly (2,1,3) and (2,3,1) are disjoint.) This gives 2 disjoint pairs per group. There are 3 groups (x = 2, y = 2, and z = 2), so within groups we get 3×2 = 6 pairs.

One must also count pairs taken from different groups. A short check shows that if one edge cube comes from the group with x = 2 and another from the group with y = 2, then the condition for disjointness forces a unique choice in the second group (depending on the z–coordinate of the first). In fact one may show that there are 8 such pairs from each pair of groups. (There are 3 pairs of groups, so 3×8 = 24 pairs from different groups.)

Thus the total number of edge–edge pairs with disjoint face–sets is 6 + 24 = 30.

──────────────────────────────
C. Adding It Up

The only cases that can produce exactly 4 visible red faces are the four cases above. Their counts are:

 • Corner–corner: 12
 • Corner–edge:  48
 • Corner–face–center: 24
 • Edge–edge:   30

Adding these gives 12 + 48 + 24 + 30 = 114.

──────────────────────────────
D. Final Answer

Thus, there are 114 ways to choose positions for the 2 red cubes among the 27 so that exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the 3×3×3 cube show red.

Answer: 114.

(A “face” here means one of the 6 large faces of the cube.) Two cubes are “visible” on a given face if that cube lies in one of the 9 unit‐cube positions that touch that face. (Rotations and reflections count as different, so we treat positions as distinct.)

A key observation is that only cubes on the boundary of the 3×3×3 can show red. (The single interior cube, at (2,2,2) if we label coordinates 1,2,3, touches no face.) In fact, if a cube is on the boundary its “visible‐face set” is determined by those coordinates equal to 1 or 3. In our 3×3×3 the cubes fall into four types:
 
• Corner cubes (8 of them): They lie at a vertex and touch 3 faces.
• Edge cubes (12 of them): They lie along an edge but are not corners and touch 2 faces.
• Face–center cubes (6 of them): They lie in the middle of a face (but not on an edge) and touch 1 face.
• Interior cube (1 of them): Touches 0 faces.
 
Since a red cube that is interior would contribute 0 visible faces, and the maximum any boundary cube gives is 3 (for a corner), it is clear that if one red cube were interior the union of the two red cubes’ visible faces would have size at most 3. Thus both red cubes must be chosen from the 26 boundary cubes.

For any red cube placed in a given position P let F(P) be the set of faces that “see” P. (For example, a corner cube at (1,1,1) “shows” the faces x = 1, y = 1, and z = 1.) When two red cubes are placed in positions P and Q the red is visible on the set 
  F(P) ∪ F(Q).
We require that |F(P) ∪ F(Q)| = 4.

Because the cubes come in three “types” (by number of faces shown) – corner (3 faces), edge (2 faces), and face–center (1 face) – one may show that the only possibilities for a pair (P,Q) (with P and Q chosen from the boundary) that yield a union of 4 faces are as follows. Writing “(a,b)” for a pair in which one cube is of type “a” and the other of type “b” (with a ≤ b so that order does not matter):

1. (Corner, Corner): Each shows 3 faces. For two corners the union has size 3+3–(number shared). To get 4 we must have
  3 + 3 – (shared) = 4 ⟹ shared = 2.
Two distinct corner cubes share exactly 2 faces precisely when they lie on a common edge. (For example, the cubes at (1,1,1) and (3,1,1) share the faces y = 1 and z = 1.) Since a cube has 12 edges and each edge has exactly 2 corner cubes, there are 12 such pairs.

  3 + 1 – (shared) = 4 ⟹ shared = 0.

We wish to choose two of the 27 unit cubes to be red (the other 25 will be white) so that when the 3×3×3 “big‐cube” is assembled the red “shows up” on exactly 4 of its 6 faces. (Here “shows up” means that on that face at least one red unit cube is visible.) In what follows we count the number of placements of the two red cubes (with the red cubes considered “indistinguishable”) that yield exactly 4 visible red faces. (Since rotations and reflections count as different, we do not have to “mod out” by symmetries.)

A key observation is that a red cube that is not on the exterior does not contribute any red to any face. (There is exactly one interior cube in a 3×3×3.) Thus if one red cube were interior the only visible red would come from the other red cube – and a cube on the surface can show on at most 3 faces (if it is a corner). Hence both red cubes must lie on the surface.

On the surface a unit cube may lie in one of three types of positions:
 • A “corner” cube (there are 8) touches 3 faces.
 • An “edge‐cube” (but not a corner; there are 12) touches 2 faces.
 • A “face–center” (there are 6) touches 1 face.

Denote by F(P) the set of faces that a red cube in position P “shows on.” (For example, a cube at a corner (say, at (1,1,1) if we label coordinates 1,2,3) shows on the three faces x=1, y=1, and z=1.) If the two red cubes are in positions P and Q then the red is visible on the set
  F(P) ∪ F(Q).
We require that |F(P) ∪ F(Q)| = 4.

It turns out that when both cubes are on the surface the only possibilities (by a short case–check) are as follows. (In what follows the “type” of a cube is recorded by the number of faces it shows on.)

1. Two corner cubes (each shows 3 faces).  
 A corner cube “sees” 3 faces. If two corners have union of 4 faces then they must share exactly 2 faces (since 3+3–|intersection| = 4 forces |intersection| = 2). Two different corner cubes share exactly 2 faces exactly when they lie on a common edge of the big cube. (For example, the cubes at (1,1,1) and (1,1,3) share the faces x=1 and y=1.)  
 Each edge of the big cube has 2 corner cubes and there are 12 edges. Thus the number of unordered pairs of corners that work is 12.

2. One corner cube and one edge cube.  
 A corner shows 3 faces and an edge cube shows 2 faces. Their union has size 3+2–|F(corner)∩F(edge)|. To have union 4 we need  
  3+2–|intersection| = 4 ⟹ |intersection| = 1.  
 A careful check shows that if you fix a corner (say, (1,1,1) whose faces are {x=1,y=1,z=1}) then among the 12 edge cubes exactly 6 have the property that they share exactly one face with the corner. (For example, the edge cube at (2,1,3) shows on {y=1,z=3} and meets the corner in the face y=1; while the edge cube at (2,1,1) shows on {y=1,z=1} and meets the corner in 2 faces.)  
 Since every corner works the same way, the total number in this case is 8×6 = 48.

3. One corner cube and one face–center cube.  
 A corner shows 3 faces and a face–center shows 1 face. Their union has size 3+1–|intersection|. To get 4 we need  
  3+1–|intersection| = 4 ⟹ |intersection| = 0.  
 A face–center is on exactly one face. (For example, (2,2,1) is the center of the face z=1.) For a given corner (say, (1,1,1) with faces {x=1,y=1,z=1}) the face–center (2,2,d) will share a face with the corner if d = 1; and similarly the other two types of face–centers (those of the form (2,d,2) and (d,2,2)) will share a face if d equals 1 or 3 appropriately. In fact one may check that for any given corner exactly 3 of the 6 face–centers have no common face with it.  
 Thus the total number in this case is 8×3 = 24.

4. Two edge cubes.  
 Each edge cube shows 2 faces so that if they shared no face the union would have size 2+2 = 4. (If they shared 1 face the union would have size 3, and if they shared 0 faces it would be 4; note that sharing 0 faces is what we need.)

We wish to build a 3×3×3 cube from 27 unit cubes – 2 red and 25 white – and we require that when the large cube is “assembled” the red cubes show on exactly 4 of the 6 faces. (In other words, if you look at the exterior of the big cube, red appears on 4 faces and white on the other 2.) (Also note that rotations and reflections count as different, so we do not “mod out” by symmetry.)

A key observation is that a red cube “shows” on a face exactly when it is placed in a unit cube that touches that face. (A unit cube in the 3×3×3 has 3, 2, 1, or 0 faces exposed depending on its position.) In our 3×3×3 cube the positions fall into four types:

1. Corners. There are 8 corners. A corner cube touches 3 faces.
2. Edges (but not corners). There are 12 edge cubes. An edge cube touches 2 faces.
3. Face‐centers (but not on an edge). There are 6 such cubes. A face–center touches 1 face.
4. The single interior cube (2,2,2) touches 0 faces.

Since a red cube that is not on the surface would not show at all, and because a single red cube on the surface shows on at most 3 faces, it is impossible for the two red cubes (if one were interior or one were a face–center) to “cover” 4 faces by themselves. (For example, a corner shows 3 faces and a face–center shows 1 face; if the other cube were interior, its contribution would be 0, and 3+0 = 3, not 4.) Thus both red cubes must be placed on the surface. (In other words, both must be among the 26 cubes that actually show on at least one face.)

Now, note that every red cube “contributes” the set of faces on which it lies. (For instance, a cube at a corner with coordinates (1,1,1) shows on the faces x = 1, y = 1, and z = 1.) If the two red cubes are in positions P and Q with “face–signatures” S(P) and S(Q) (each a subset of {x = 1, x = 3, y = 1, y = 3, z = 1, z = 3}), then the red is seen on the set S(P) ∪ S(Q). We require that
  |S(P) ∪ S(Q)| = 4.

It turns out that when you look at the possible types of positions (corner, edge, face–center) the only pairs (P,Q) that can yield a union of 4 faces are those in which the two cubes are chosen from among the following cases:

• Both are corners.
• One is a corner and the other is an edge.
• One is a corner and the other is a face–center.
• Both are edges.

(Any pair involving a face–center with an edge or two face–centers would yield a union of size at most 3.)

Let’s analyze each case.

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. Two Corners

A corner cube has signature of size 3. If P and Q are two distinct corners then
  |S(P) ∪ S(Q)| = 3 + 3 – |S(P) ∩ S(Q)|.
Since two different corners cannot share all 3 faces (that would force them to be identical), the possible intersection sizes are 0, 1, or 2. For the union to have 4 elements we need
  6 – |S(P) ∩ S(Q)| = 4  ⟹ |S(P) ∩ S(Q)| = 2.
In other words, the two corner cubes must share exactly 2 of their 3 faces. (For example, the corner at (1,1,1) and the corner at (3,1,1) share the faces y = 1 and z = 1.) 

Now, fix any corner (say, (1,1,1)). Which other corners share exactly 2 faces with it? They must differ in exactly one coordinate. From (1,1,1) the possibilities are (3,1,1), (1,3,1), and (1,1,3) – a total of 3. Since the 8 corners are symmetric, the total number of unordered pairs is
  (8 × 3) / 2 = 12.
──────────────────────────────
Case 2. One Corner and One Edge

An edge cube (one of the 12) has signature of size 2. If P is a corner (size 3) and Q is an edge (size 2) then
  |S(P) ∪ S(Q)| = 3 + 2 – |S(P) ∩ S(Q)|.
We need this to equal 4 so that
  5 – |S(P) ∩ S(Q)| = 4  ⟹ |S(P) ∩ S(Q)| = 1.
That is, the corner and the edge must share exactly 1 face.

To count these, fix a corner. (For example, take (1,1,1) whose signature is {x = 1, y = 1, z = 1}.) An edge cube is one that has exactly one coordinate equal to 2 and the other two equal to 1 or 3. There are three “types” depending on which coordinate is 2. For instance:

We wish to “paint” two of the 27 unit cubes red (the other 25 white) and then “glue” them together to form a 3×3×3 cube so that when the big cube is viewed from the outside exactly 4 of its 6 faces show at least one red cube. (Here rotations and reflections count as different assemblies.) In what follows the red cubes are “indistinguishable” (only their color matters) and we count an assembly by the locations of the red cubes.

An important observation is that a red cube that is not on the surface does not “show” at all. (The only interior cube is the very center, at (2,2,2) in a natural coordinate system.) In fact, if one red cube were interior then the only red “visibility” would come from the other red cube – but a cube on a face can show on at most 3 faces (if it is a corner) and on 1 or 2 faces (if it is a face‐center or edge–cube, respectively). Hence, to have red visible on 4 faces the two red cubes must both lie on the surface (that is, in one of the 26 “boundary” positions).

To set up a coordinate system let the positions in the big cube be given by (i, j, k) with i, j, k ∈ {1, 2, 3}. Then the 6 faces are 
  x = 1, x = 3, y = 1, y = 3, z = 1, z = 3.
A unit cube at (i, j, k) “shows” on the face x = 1 if i = 1, on x = 3 if i = 3, etc.

Thus the set of faces visible from a given cube is determined by which of its coordinates equal 1 or 3. (For example, a cube at (2,1,3) shows on y = 1 and z = 3.) Notice that:
 • A “face–center” cube (like (2,1,2), (2,2,1), etc.) has exactly one coordinate equal to 1 or 3 and so “contributes” 1 face.
 • An “edge” cube (like (2,1,1) or (1,2,3), but not a corner) has exactly two coordinates equal to 1 or 3 and so contributes 2 faces.
 • A “corner” cube (like (1,1,1), etc.) has three such coordinates and contributes 3 faces.

However, when two red cubes are used the red “visibility” on a given face occurs if at least one red cube lies on that face. (Even if both lie on the same face the face is counted only once.) Thus if we denote by F(p) the set of faces shown by a red cube at position p, then the assembled big cube shows red on exactly 4 faces if and only if

  |F(p) ∪ F(q)| = 4.

A very systematic way to count the number of pairs {p,q} (with p and q chosen from the 26 surface positions) that yield exactly 4 visible faces is to “encode” the contribution of each cube by its coordinates. (It is most convenient to work with ordered pairs and then divide by 2 at the end since the red cubes are identical.)

Step 1. Associate to each coordinate (i, j, k) the following rule:
 – For the x–coordinate, a cube shows on x = 1 if i = 1 and on x = 3 if i = 3.
 – Similarly for y and z.

Thus if a cube has coordinate i it “contributes” 0 to the x–side if i = 2, contributes 1 if i is 1 or 3 (but note that if both cubes happen to be 1 or both 3 the face is still counted once). In other words, if we look at an ordered pair of x–coordinates (a, b) (with a, b ∈ {1,2,3}) then we define its “contribution” f(a,b) as follows:
  • f(2,2) = 0       (neither shows an x–face)
  • f(2,1) = f(1,2) = 1   (one shows x = 1)
  • f(2,3) = f(3,2) = 1   (one shows x = 3)
  • f(1,1) = f(3,3) = 1   (both show the same face, still 1 face)
  • f(1,3) = f(3,1) = 2   (one shows x = 1 and the other x = 3, so both faces appear)

A similar rule holds for the y– and z–coordinates.

Step 2. For a given ordered pair of red cubes (p, q) the total number of distinct red faces visible is the sum of the contributions from the x–, y–, and z–coordinates:
  Total = f(pₓ, qₓ) + f(p_y, q_y) + f(p_z, q_z).

We want exactly 4 visible faces, i.e.
  f(pₓ, qₓ) + f(p_y, q_y) + f(p_z, q_z) = 4.

Step 3. Notice that the choices on different coordinates are “independent” (after all a cube’s coordinates come from independent sets {1,2,3}). For one coordinate the 9 ordered pairs (a, b) (with a, b ∈ {1,2,3}) break down as follows:
  • 1 possibility gives contribution 0: (2,2).
  • 6 possibilities give contribution 1: (2,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,2), (1,1), (3,3).
  • 2 possibilities give contribution 2: (1,3) and (3,1).

Thus for one coordinate the “weight–generating function” is
  G(t) = 1 + 6t + 2t².

Since the three coordinates act independently, the generating function for the total contribution is
  G(t)³ = (1 + 6t + 2t²)³.
We want the coefficient of t⁴ in this expansion.

Step 4. Find the coefficient of t⁴ in (1 + 6t + 2t²)³.
One may do this by “counting in cases.” In an ordered triple (cₓ, c_y, c_z) where each c is 0, 1, or 2 and cₓ + c_y + c_z = 4, the only possibilities are:
  (a) One coordinate contributes 0 and the other two contribute 2 each. (For example, (0,2,2).)
  (b) One coordinate contributes 2 and the other two contribute 1 each. (For example, (2,1,1).)

For case (a): 
 – For the coordinate with 0 the number of ordered pairs is 1.
 – For each coordinate with 2 the number is 2.
Thus for a fixed assignment (say x gives 0, y and z give 2) the number is 1×2×2 = 4.
There are 3 ways to choose which coordinate is 0, so the total from case (a) is 3×4 = 12.

For case (b):
 – For the coordinate with 2 the number is 2.
 – For each coordinate with 1 the number is 6.
Thus for a fixed assignment (say x gives 2, y and z give 1) the number is 2×6×6 = 72.
There are 3 ways to choose which coordinate gets the 2, so the total from case (b) is 3×72 = 216.

Thus the total number of ordered pairs (p, q) (with p and q chosen from all 27 positions, but note that if one cube were interior then its coordinate would be 2 in every slot – and such pairs would yield a total contribution of 0; they are not “dangerous” here because 0 ≠ 4) that yield exactly 4 visible faces is
  12 + 216 = 228.

Step 5. Finally, since the two red cubes are identical the order does not matter. (Our count of 228 was for ordered pairs.) Thus the number of assemblies is
  228/2 = 114.

A few remarks:
 • One may worry that a red cube placed in an “interior” position (like (2,2,2)) would ruin the count. In fact, if one red cube were interior then its contribution in every coordinate would be 0 and the total visible faces would come solely from the other cube – which can contribute at most 3 faces. Hence both red cubes must be on the surface.
 • One may also check by “by hand” (grouping by the types of cubes – face–centers, edges, and corners) that no other configuration can yield exactly 4 visible faces.

Thus, the number of ways to choose positions for the 2 red cubes (among the 27 positions) so that exactly 4 faces of the 3×3×3 cube show red is 114.

Answer: 114.

We will show that when two red unit cubes (and 25 white ones) are placed into the 3×3×3 “big‐cube” (so that all 27 unit cubes are used) in such a way that exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the big cube show red, there are exactly 114 assemblies (with rotations and reflections considered distinct).

In what follows we describe one way to “see” the answer.

──────────────────────────────
A “big‐picture” view

Label the 6 faces of the big cube “front, back, left, right, top, bottom.” In any placement the red cubes “contribute” red to those faces on which they lie. (A red cube that is not on the surface shows no red.) Since we want exactly 4 faces to be “red‐visible” the union of the sets of faces touched by the red cubes must be a 4–element subset R ⊂ {front,back,left,right,top,bottom} (and the other 2 faces, call them S, get no red).

An important observation is that if even one red cube is hidden inside (i.e. not on the surface) then its contribution is empty. In that case the other red cube (even if on an edge or corner) can touch at most 3 faces. Hence both red cubes must lie on the surface.

Now, note that the 3×3×3 cube has 27 cubes, exactly one of which is completely interior; the other 26 are “surface cubes.” (These 26 come in three types:
 • 8 corners (each touches 3 faces),
 • 12 edge–cubes (each touches 2 faces),
 • 6 face–centers (each touches 1 face).)

For a given choice of R (a set of 4 faces to be red) the condition that “red is visible on exactly those 4 faces” forces that
 (1) neither red cube may touch any face in the complement S (of size 2), and
 (2) the two red cubes (each on the surface) must “cover” R (that is, every face in R is touched by at least one red cube).

Thus if we fix R then we are allowed to use only those surface cubes whose set of faces (that is, the faces on which the unit cube lies) is a subset of R. (For example, if R = {front, right, top, left} then a red cube placed at a corner that touches front, right and top is “allowed” but one that touches back is not.) Then among the allowed positions we must choose 2 so that the union of their “face–sets” is exactly R.

A key point is that the answer will depend on R. (In fact, every 4–element subset R arises as the set of faces that are “red‐visible” in some configuration.) However, by symmetry the answer depends only on the “type” of R. In any 4–subset R the two faces not in R (namely S = the complement) are either opposite or adjacent. (There are 3 pairs of opposite faces and 12 pairs of adjacent faces among the 6 faces.) One may show that when S is a pair of opposite faces the number of placements (of the two red cubes among the allowed positions) is 2, and when S is a pair of adjacent faces the number is 9.

We will show that when two red unit cubes are placed in the 27 positions of a 3×3×3 cube (with the other 25 cubes white), the number of placements for which exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the large cube show red is 114. (Here “red is visible on a face” means that at least one red cube lies in a unit‐cube position on that face; note that rotations and reflections count as different.)

In what follows the “big cube” has faces in the “x–, y–, and z–directions.” (For example, the “left” face is x = 1, the “right” face is x = 3, the “front” is y = 1, the “back” is y = 3, the “bottom” is z = 1, and the “top” is z = 3.) A unit cube in position (x, y, z) (with each coordinate 1, 2, or 3) shows a red face on the x–side if x = 1 (showing the “left” face) or if x = 3 (showing the “right” face); similarly for y and z.

An important observation is that a red cube contributes to a face only when its coordinate in that direction is 1 or 3. (For example, a cube at (2,2,2) is completely hidden from the outside.) Thus, if a red cube is at (x, y, z) its “visible‐face set” is
  { L if x = 1, R if x = 3, F if y = 1, B if y = 3, D if z = 1, U if z = 3 }.
When two red cubes are placed, the red “picture” on the outside is the union of the two sets. We want exactly 4 distinct faces to appear in that union.

A very efficient way to count the placements is to “break up” the 3‐dimensional count into three independent 1–dimensional counts (one for each coordinate). (Remember that the two red cubes are “labeled” by position; later we will pass to unordered pairs since the cubes are identical.)

Step 1. Count the contribution from one coordinate (say x).

A cube’s x–coordinate is 1, 2, or 3. For an ordered pair of cubes (that is, choosing an x–coordinate for cube A and an x–coordinate for cube B, with the cubes considered distinct) the possibilities and the “visible‐face” outcome in the x–direction are as follows:

  • If both coordinates equal 2 then neither cube “shows” an x–face. (Outcome: ∅, “size” 0.)
  • If one coordinate is 2 and the other is 1 then the union is {1} (that is, the left face appears). (Outcome: size 1.)
  • Similarly, if one coordinate is 2 and the other is 3 the union is {3} (right face). (Size 1.)
  • If both are 1 then the union is {1} (size 1).
  • If both are 3 then the union is {3} (size 1).
  • If one coordinate is 1 and the other is 3 then the union is {1, 3} (both left and right appear). (Size 2.)

Thus, when we list all 9 ordered pairs (since 3 choices for cube A and 3 for cube B) we get:
  (1,1): size 1
  (1,2): size 1
  (1,3): size 2
  (2,1): size 1
  (2,2): size 0
  (2,3): size 1
  (3,1): size 2
  (3,2): size 1
  (3,3): size 1

So for the x–direction the counts are:

──────────────────────────────

Subtracting, the number of edge–edge pairs with no common face is

──────────────────────────────
Other Cases
──────────────────────────────
One might also consider a pair consisting of an edge cube and a face–center cube. However, an edge cube shows on 2 faces and a face–center on 1 face. Total Count
──────────────────────────────
Adding the counts from the valid cases we get:
  Case 1: 12
  Case 2: 48
  Case 3: 24
  Case 4: 30
Total = 12 + 48 + 24 + 30 = 114.

Therefore, there are 114 ways to choose positions for the 2 red cubes (with the remaining 25 white cubes filling the rest) so that red is visible on exactly 4 faces of the 3×3×3 cube.

Answer: 114.

Because a unit cube that is not on the surface does not show on any face, at least one red cube must lie on the surface. In fact, since a single boundary cube can show on at most 3 faces (a corner cube shows on 3 faces, an edge‐cube on 2, and a face–center on 1), the only way to “cover” 4 faces is to use two cubes that lie on the boundary and whose sets of “visible faces” (that is, the faces of the big cube that they touch) have a union of size 4.

It is convenient to classify the boundary cubes by how many faces they touch. In a 3×3×3 cube the positions are as follows:

• Face–center cubes (touch 1 face): There are 6 of these. (For example, the cube at (1,2,2) touches only the face x = 1.)

• Edge cubes (touch 2 faces): There are 12. (For example, (1,1,2) touches the faces x = 1 and y = 1.)

• Corner cubes (touch 3 faces): There are 8. (For example, (1,1,1) touches x = 1, y = 1, and z = 1.)

Now, if a red cube is placed in a given boundary position it “contributes” the set of faces it touches. Suppose one red cube “covers” a set A of faces and the other covers a set B. Then the red appears on the union A ∪ B of faces. We want

  |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| – |A ∩ B| = 4.

Since the possible sizes are 1, 2, or 3 (for face–center, edge, and corner, respectively), one may check that the only possibilities (with |A| ≤ |B|) are:

1. One cube is a face–center (|A| = 1) and the other is a corner (|B| = 3) with A and B disjoint. (Then 1 + 3 – 0 = 4.)

2. Both cubes are edge cubes (|A| = |B| = 2) with A and B disjoint. (Then 2 + 2 – 0 = 4.)

3. One cube is an edge (2 faces) and the other a corner (3 faces) with the two sets sharing exactly 1 face. (Then 2 + 3 – 1 = 4.)

4. Both cubes are corners (3 faces each) and they share exactly 2 faces. (Then 3 + 3 – 2 = 4.)

We now count the number of unordered pairs (of positions for the red cubes) in each case.

───────────────────────────── 
Case 1. (Face–center, Corner with disjoint sets)

A face–center cube touches exactly 1 face. For a given face–center (say the one on the x = 1 face, at (1,2,2)) the “forbidden” corner cubes are those that also touch that same face. There are 12 edge cubes. (One may check that each edge cube “lives” in a unique position on the surface and has a 2–element set of faces.) Case 4. (Corner, Corner with intersection of size 2)

Adding the counts from the four cases we get

We wish to choose two of the 27 unit cubes to be red so that when the 3×3×3 cube is assembled the “red‐visible” faces (i.e. the faces of the large cube that show a red unit cube) number exactly 4. (Here “rotations and reflections are considered distinct”, so we are simply “labeling” positions.)

A key observation is that only cubes on the surface can show red. (The single “interior” cube is hidden from view.) In a 3×3×3 cube the surface positions break into three types:
 
• Corners (8 cubes) – each touches 3 faces.
• Edge–centers (12 cubes) – each touches 2 faces.
• Face–centers (6 cubes) – each touches 1 face.

If a red cube is placed in an interior position it would not be seen at all. And if only one red cube is on the surface the total number of red–visible faces is at most 3. Thus both red cubes must lie on the surface.

Now, if a red cube is placed at a surface position it “contributes” the set of faces on which it lies. For example, a corner at (1,1,1) (using coordinates x,y,z with 1 or 3 on the surface) shows the faces x=1, y=1, and z=1. When two red cubes are placed, the set of faces that “show red” is the union of the face–sets of the two cubes. We want this union to have exactly 4 elements.

A useful way to organize the count is to break the possibilities according to the types of the two red cubes. (Remember that the cubes are “labeled” only by position so that an unordered pair is a configuration.) In what follows the “face–set” of a cube is the set of the 6 faces of the large cube that it touches. (We denote the faces by L (x=1), R (x=3), F (y=1), B (y=3), Bo (z=1), and T (z=3).)

A short calculation shows that if a cube of type
  • corner (3 faces) and a cube of type
  • edge (2 faces)
are used, then in order for
  |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| – |A ∩ B| 
to equal 4 we must have
  3 + 2 – |A ∩ B| = 4 ⟹ |A ∩ B| = 1.
Similarly, if one cube is a face–center (1 face) and the other a corner (3 faces) then to have 1+3–|A∩B| = 4 we need |A ∩ B| = 0.
Finally, if both are edges (each 2 faces) then we need 2+2–|A∩B| = 4 so that |A∩B| = 0.
(One may check that no pair involving two face–centers can ever yield 4 distinct faces.)

Thus the only cases that can work are:

 Case 1. Two red cubes both at corners with the property that their face–sets intersect in exactly 2 faces.
 Case 2. One red cube at a corner and the other at an edge with the property that their face–sets intersect in exactly 1 face.
 Case 3. One red cube at a face–center and the other at a corner with the property that their face–sets are disjoint (intersection of size 0).
 Case 4. Two red cubes both at edges with disjoint face–sets (intersection 0).

We now describe one way to count the number of pairs (remember the cubes are “unlabeled” so we count unordered pairs):

──────────────────────────────
Step 1. Count (corner, corner) pairs with intersection 2

A corner cube touches 3 faces. Two different corners will share exactly 2 faces precisely when they are “adjacent” along an edge of the large cube. (For example, the corners (1,1,1) with faces {L, F, Bo} and (1,1,3) with {L, F, T} share {L, F}.) Each edge of the big cube has exactly 2 corner cubes and they form one such pair. ──────────────────────────────
Step 2. Count (corner, edge) pairs with intersection 1

An edge–center cube touches 2 faces. For a given edge cube the condition is that its 2 faces and a corner’s 3 faces must share exactly 1 face. (For example, an edge cube at (1,1,2) has faces {L, F}. A corner such as (1,3,1) has {L, B, Bo} and the intersection is {L}.) One may check by going through the 12 edge positions (which fall into 3 groups of 4) that for each edge cube there are exactly 4 corner cubes (out of the 8) giving an intersection of size 1. Thus the total from this case is 12×4 = 48.
──────────────────────────────
Step 3. Count (face–center, corner) pairs with intersection 0

A face–center cube touches exactly 1 face. For the union to have 4 faces when joined with a corner (which touches 3) we must have no overlap. For example, if the face–center is on the L face (position (1,2,2) with face set {L}), then a corner must not touch L – that is, it must lie on the opposite side (x = 3). There are 4 such corners. Since there are 6 face–centers, this case contributes 6×4 = 24.
──────────────────────────────
Step 4. Count (edge, edge) pairs with intersection 0

There are 12 edge cubes. One may show by a short analysis (or by symmetry) that if you list the 12 edge cubes and count, exactly 30 unordered pairs of them have disjoint face–sets. (For example, an edge cube at (1,1,2) has faces {L, F} and it will be disjoint from an edge cube such as (3,? ,?) whose faces are {R, …} but not sharing L or F.)
──────────────────────────────
Step 5. Add the cases

Now add the numbers from the four cases:
  Case 1: 12
  Case 2: 48
  Case 3: 24
  Case 4: 30
Total = 12 + 48 + 24 + 30 = 114.
──────────────────────────────
Thus, there are 114 ways to choose two surface positions for the red cubes so that exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the large cube show red.

Answer: 114.
