We wish to choose two of the 27 unit cubes to be red (all others white) and “assemble” them into a 3×3×3 cube so that when the big cube is viewed from the outside exactly 4 of its 6 faces show at least one red unit‐cube. (Here rotations and reflections count as different, so we do not “mod out” by symmetry.) One may show that in any valid placement both red cubes must lie on the surface (if one were interior its “red” would not be seen) and that, when restricted to the 26 surface positions, the only possibilities (by “type”) are:

• A corner cube (touching 3 faces). There are 8 such positions.
• An edge cube (but not a corner; it lies in the middle of an edge) touching 2 faces. There are 12 such positions.
• A face–center cube (in the middle of a face) touching 1 face. There are 6 such positions.

If a red cube sits at a given position it “contributes” the faces on which it lies. (For example, a cube at a corner where x = 1, y = 3, z = 3 shows on the faces x = 1, y = 3, and z = 3.) In any placement the “red–visible” faces are just the union of the faces shown by the two red cubes. We require that exactly 4 distinct faces appear.

A useful idea is to “group” the two red cubes by the numbers of faces they show. (Call these “types”: 3, 2, or 1.) Then if one red cube shows m faces and the other shows n faces, their union has size m + n minus the number of faces common to both. (Two cubes may “share” a face if they both lie on that same face of the big cube.) In our situation the only possibilities (with m+n at least 4) turn out to be:

  (3,3), (3,2), (2,2) and (3,1).

We now explain how to count the valid pairs in each case.

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. Both cubes are corners (each shows 3 faces).

A corner cube (with all three coordinates equal to 1 or 3) shows the three faces determined by its coordinates. If the two corners are A = (a, b, c) and B = (d, e, f) (with each coordinate 1 or 3) then they “share” a face in coordinate i exactly when a = d = (1 or 3) (and similarly for y and z). In other words the union has size 
  6 – (number of coordinates in which the two cubes agree).
For the union to have exactly 4 faces we need
  6 – (number of equal coordinates) = 4 ⟹ number of equal coordinates = 2.
But two distinct corners share exactly 2 coordinates precisely when they are the two endpoints of the same edge. (For example, (1,1,1) and (1,1,3) share the x– and y–coordinates.) Since a cube has 12 edges, there are 12 unordered pairs of corners with union size 4.

──────────────────────────────
Case 2. One cube is a corner (3 faces) and the other is an edge cube (2 faces).

An edge cube is one that lies in the middle of an edge. (For example, a cube of the form (2, b, c) with b,c ∈ {1,3} is an edge cube; similarly there are types with the 2 in the y– or z–coordinate.) Note that an edge cube “shows” exactly the two faces corresponding to its two boundary coordinates.

Now, suppose the corner is at (a, b, c) (with a, b, c ∈ {1,3}) and the edge cube is, say, of the form (2, b′, c′) (so it lies on the two faces corresponding to y and z). Since the corner does not lie on any face in the x–direction the only possible overlaps come from comparing the y– and z–coordinates. For the union to have size 3 + 2 – (overlap) = 4 we must have exactly one common face; that is, exactly one of b = b′ or c = c′ must hold. (For example, if (a, b, c) = (1,1,1) and the edge cube is (2,1,3) then the common face is the one with y = 1, and the union is {x = 1, y = 1, z = 1, z = 3}.) 

A short check shows that for a fixed corner there are 2 choices for an edge cube of a given “type” (that is, with the 2 in a specified coordinate) and since there are 3 types (the 2 may occur in the x–, y–, or z–coordinate) there are 3×2 = 6 valid edge cubes for that corner. With 8 corners the total number of unordered (corner,edge) pairs is 8×6 = 48.

──────────────────────────────
Case 3. Both cubes are edge cubes (each shows 2 faces).

An edge cube shows exactly the 2 faces that contain the edge on which it lies. (For example, the edge cube (2,1,1) shows the faces y = 1 and z = 1.) For two edge cubes the union has size 2 + 2 minus the number of faces they share. To have union size 4 we must have no common face. (If they shared one face the union would have size 3, and if they were on the same edge they would share both faces giving union size 2.)

It turns out that if we identify each edge cube with the edge of the big cube on which it sits (and there are 12 edges) then two different edges yield disjoint sets of faces precisely when the two edges do not lie on a common face. A short counting shows that among the C(12,2) = 66 pairs of edges, exactly 36 pairs lie on a common face (each face has 4 edges and any two of these 4 share that face) so that the number of pairs with no common face is 66 – 36 = 30.

──────────────────────────────
Case 4. One cube is a corner (3 faces) and the other is a face–center (1 face).

A face–center cube (such as (1,2,2) on the face x = 1) shows exactly 1 face. For the union of a corner (which shows 3 faces) and a face–center to have size 4 we must have no overlap; that is, the single face shown by the face–center must not be one of the 3 faces shown by the corner. For a given face (say, x = 1) the corner cubes that do not touch that face are exactly those with x = 3 (and then y and z can be 1 or 3, giving 2×2 = 4 possibilities). Since there are 6 faces (and hence 6 face–center positions) the total number of unordered (corner,face–center) pairs is 6×4 = 24.

──────────────────────────────
No other combinations can yield a union of 4 faces. (For example, two face–centers would show at most 2 faces and an edge together with a face–center would show at most 3 faces.)

Adding the counts from the four cases we get:
  Case 1: 12 
  Case 2: 48 
  Case 3: 30 
  Case 4: 24 
for a grand total of 12 + 48 + 30 + 24 = 114.

Thus, there are 114 ways to choose positions for the 2 red cubes (among the 26 surface positions) so that exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the 3×3×3 cube show red.

──────────────────────────────
Answer: 114.

We will show that if you “paint” two of the 27 unit‐cubes red (and the other 25 white) and then “glue” them together to form a 3×3×3 cube, then in order that exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the big cube show some red, the two red cubes must lie on the exterior and – when you “look” at the set of faces on which each red cube appears – the union of their “red‐face sets” has exactly 4 elements. (In our count the red cubes are “indistinguishable”, and rotations/reflections count as different.)

In what follows we explain one way to analyze the situation and show that the answer is 114.

──────────────────────────────
A. The “Face–set” idea

Label the 3×3×3 positions by coordinates (x,y,z) with each coordinate 1, 2, or 3. (The “big” cube has faces 
  x = 1, x = 3, y = 1, y = 3, z = 1, z = 3.)
A unit cube on the surface (i.e. with at least one coordinate equal to 1 or 3) “shows” red on each face on which it lies. For example:
 • A “face–center” cube (one that lies in the center of a face) has exactly one coordinate equal to 1 or 3 and so shows red on 1 face.
 • An “edge” cube (one that lies along an edge but is not a corner) has exactly two coordinates equal to 1 or 3 and so shows red on 2 faces.
 • A “corner” cube has three coordinates equal to 1 or 3 and so shows red on 3 faces.

A red cube placed in an interior position (with all coordinates 2) would show no red at all. (Also, if one red cube were interior and the other on the surface, then at most 3 faces would be red – too few.) Thus both red cubes must lie on the surface. (There are 26 surface cubes in all.)

Now, if a red cube is placed in a given surface position it “contributes” its set of visible faces. (For example, a cube at (1,2,2) shows only the face x = 1.) If the two red cubes lie in positions A and B with visible–face sets F(A) and F(B) then the overall set of faces showing red is 
  F(A) ∪ F(B).
We require that
  |F(A) ∪ F(B)| = 4.
Since for a cube on the surface the number of faces it shows is 1 (if it is a face–center), 2 (if it is on an edge) or 3 (if it is a corner), one may check that the only possibilities (with a = |F(A)| and b = |F(B)|) are:
  (1,3), (2,2), (2,3) and (3,3)
with the extra condition that
  a + b – |F(A) ∩ F(B)| = 4.
One may verify that these force
  • For a (1,3) pair: the face–center and the corner must “miss” each other (i.e. the corner is not on the one face of the face–center).
  • For a (2,2) pair: the two edge cubes must have no face in common.
  • For a (2,3) pair: an edge cube and a corner must share exactly one face.
  • For a (3,3) pair: the two corner cubes must share exactly 2 faces (that is, they must be the two endpoints of some edge).

We now count the number of ordered pairs (with the two red cubes considered “unlabeled”) in each case.

──────────────────────────────
B. Counting by type

(1) Red cubes of types (face–center, corner):

• A face–center cube lies in the center of one face. (There are 6 faces so 6 such cubes.)
• A corner cube lies at a corner. (There are 8 corners.)
Now, a given face–center (say on the face x = 1) shows red only on that face. In order that the union of the two cubes’ red–faces have size 4 the corner cube must not lie on that same face. (On a given face there are 4 corners.) Thus for each face–center there are 8 – 4 = 4 acceptable corner cubes.
So the total number of (face–center, corner) pairs is
  6 × 4 = 24.

(2) Red cubes of types (edge, edge):

An edge cube (one that is not a corner but lies along an edge) shows red on 2 faces. There are 12 edge cubes.
One may show (by a short “grouping‐argument” explained below) that among the 12 edge cubes the number of unordered pairs that have no face in common is 30.

A brief explanation of the grouping method:
 • Every edge cube has exactly one coordinate equal to 2 and the other two (which determine its red–faces) are either 1 or 3.
 • Group the 12 edge cubes according to which coordinate equals 2. (There are 3 groups of 4.)
 • One may check that in each group the only way for two cubes’ red–face sets to be disjoint is very “rigid” (in fact, in each group exactly 2 unordered pairs work), and that when cubes come from different groups the count works out so that overall there are 30 pairs.
Thus the (edge, edge) case gives 30 pairs.

(3) Red cubes of types (edge, corner):

An edge cube shows red on 2 faces and a corner cube on 3 faces. For their union to have 4 faces we must have
  2 + 3 – |intersection| = 4 ⟹ |intersection| = 1.
In other words the edge and the corner must share exactly one face.
Now, fix an edge cube. Its two red faces (say F and G) lie on two different faces. A corner cube lies on 3 faces. For the intersection F(A) ∩ F(B) to have exactly one element the corner must lie on exactly one of F or G (but not both). One may check that for any given edge cube the number of corner cubes lying on exactly one of its two faces is 4.
Since there are 12 edge cubes, the total number of (edge, corner) pairs is
  12 × 4 = 48.

(4) Red cubes of types (corner, corner):

A corner cube shows red on 3 faces. For two corner cubes the union will have 4 faces provided they share exactly 2 faces. But two corner cubes share 2 faces precisely when they are the two endpoints of some edge.
There are 12 edges of the big cube and each edge has 2 endpoints. Thus the number of unordered pairs is 12.

──────────────────────────────
C. Adding the cases

Now add the counts from the four cases:
  (face–center, corner): 24 
  (edge, edge):     30 
  (edge, corner):    48 
  (corner, corner):   12 
Total = 24 + 30 + 48 + 12 = 114.

──────────────────────────────
D. Conclusion

Since the red cubes are identical and the white cubes (25 of them) fill in the remaining positions in only one way, the number of assemblies of the 3×3×3 cube in which exactly 4 faces show red is 114.

Thus, the answer is 114.

In what follows rotations and reflections count as different, so we need not “mod out” by symmetry.

A key observation is that in a 3×3×3 cube the only cube that is not seen from the outside is the single interior cube at (2,2,2) (if we label positions by coordinates 1, 2, 3 in each direction). Since there is only one interior cube, the only two types of placements for the 2 red cubes are:

 Case 1. Both red cubes lie on the surface.
 Case 2. One red cube is on the surface and the other is the unique interior cube.

Let’s see which of these can yield exactly 4 red‐visible faces.

───────────────────────────── 
Step 1. Analyzing the Two Cases

• Case 2 (one red on surface, one interior):  
The interior cube does not contribute to any face. Thus the set of red–visible faces is exactly the set of faces that the surface red cube touches. But every cube on the surface lies on either a corner (touching 3 faces), an edge (touching 2 faces) or the center of a face (touching 1 face). None of these has 4 faces.  – Face–centers: 6 cubes (each touches 1 face).

 An edge cube touches 2 faces. For the union to have size 4 we need

 An edge cube is one that has exactly one coordinate equal to 2 and the other two equal to 1 or 3. One may check that for a given corner there are exactly 6 edge cubes that share exactly one face with it.

 A face–center touches 1 face. For the union to be 4 we need
  3 + 1 – |A ∩ B| = 4 ⟹ |A ∩ B| = 0.

 Each edge cube touches 2 faces. For the union to have size 4 we need
  2 + 2 – |A ∩ B| = 4 ⟹ |A ∩ B| = 0.
 That is, the two edge cubes must not share any face.

5. The remaining possibilities (one edge with one face–center or both face–centers) yield unions of size at most 3 and are not acceptable.

Step 3. Adding the Counts

Only Case 1 (both red cubes on the surface) can work. Summing the valid pairs from the subcases we have:

 Corner–Edge:   48  
 Corner–Face–center: 24  
 Edge–Edge:   30  

Total = 12 + 48 + 24 + 30 = 114.

There are 114 ways to choose two surface positions for the red cubes (out of the 26 surface cubes) so that the union of the faces on which they lie is exactly 4. (The other case, with one red cube interior, cannot yield 4 red faces.) Since rotations and reflections are considered distinct, no further division is needed.

Thus, the answer is 114.

In what follows the 27 positions are labeled by coordinates (x, y, z) with each coordinate equal to 1, 2, or 3. (For example, the cube in the “back‐left–bottom” corner is (1,1,1) and the “front–right–top” is (3,3,3).) A red cube “shows” on a face if its coordinate in the corresponding direction is 1 or 3. (Thus the face x = 1 consists of all cubes with x = 1, etc.)

An important observation is that a red cube placed in an interior position (the unique cube with coordinates (2,2,2)) would not be seen from any face. Since we want red to appear on 4 faces, both red cubes must lie on the surface.

 • A corner cube (with all coordinates 1 or 3) touches 3 faces. There are 8 corners.
 • An edge cube (with exactly one coordinate equal to 2 and the other two equal to 1 or 3) touches 2 faces. There are 12 such cubes.
 • A face‐center cube (with exactly one coordinate equal to 1 or 3 and the other two equal to 2) touches 1 face. There are 6 such cubes.

  |F(A) ∪ F(B)| = 4.
Since the maximum number of faces a single cube can cover is 3 (for a corner), the only way to get a union of 4 is to “mix” cubes that cover different numbers of faces. (In fact, if both cubes were placed in positions that cover only 1 or only 2 faces, their total would be at most 3; and two corners that do not share an edge would cover 6 faces.) Thus the only possibilities (up to reordering the two red cubes) are:

 Case 1. Both cubes are corners (each covers 3 faces).
 Case 2. One cube is a corner (3 faces) and the other is an edge (2 faces).
 Case 3. One cube is a corner (3 faces) and the other is a face‐center (1 face).
 Case 4. Both cubes are edges (each covers 2 faces).

We now count the number of pairs (remember the red cubes are identical so the order does not matter) in each case that yield a union of exactly 4 faces.

──────────────────────────────

A corner touches 3 faces. If two distinct corners are used, then
  |F(A) ∪ F(B)| = 3 + 3 – (number of faces common to both).
For the union to equal 4 we must have
  6 – (common faces) = 4 ⟹ (common faces) = 2.
Two different corners share exactly 2 faces precisely when they lie on a common edge. (For example, the corners (1,1,1) and (1,1,3) share the faces x = 1 and y = 1.) 

Each edge of the 3×3×3 cube has exactly 2 corner cubes, and there are 12 edges. Thus the number of pairs in this case is 12.

Case 2. One Corner and One Edge

A corner covers 3 faces and an edge covers 2 faces. Their union is

To have a union of 4 we need
  5 – (common faces) = 4 ⟹ (common faces) = 1.
That is, the corner and the edge must share exactly one face.

A corner covers 3 faces and a face‐center covers 1 face. Their union is

For the union to equal 4 we need

That is, the corner and the face‐center must not share any face.

A given corner (say, (1,1,1)) touches 3 faces. On each of those faces there is exactly 1 face‐center. Thus among the 6 face‐centers, 3 lie on a face that the corner touches and must be avoided. The remaining 3 face‐centers do not share any face with the corner. Hence for each corner there are 3 valid choices. With 8 corners, the total number in this case is 8 × 3 = 24.

Case 4. Two Edges

To have a union of 4 we need
  4 – (common faces) = 4 ⟹ (common faces) = 0.

Adding the Cases

Now we add the counts from the four cases:
 Case 1: 12
 Case 2: 48
 Case 3: 24
 Case 4: 42
Total = 12 + 48 + 24 + 42 = 126.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

There are 126 ways to choose positions for the 2 red cubes (with the remaining 25 white) so that exactly 4 of the 6 faces of the 3×3×3 cube show red. (Since rotations and reflections are considered distinct, we do not divide by any symmetry factor.)

We wish to build a 3×3×3 cube from 27 unit cubes – 2 red and 25 white – so that when the big cube is “assembled” the red cubes are seen on exactly 4 of its 6 faces. (Here “seen on a face” means that the red cube lies in one of the 9 unit‐cube positions on that face; note that a red cube hidden in the interior does not count.) Moreover, rotations and reflections count as different, so we treat each of the 27 positions as distinct.

Because the red cubes are only 2 in number, it is natural to “mark” the positions of the red cubes among the 27. (The white cubes fill the remaining 25 positions.) However, not every choice of 2 positions will yield exactly 4 faces showing red. (For example, if both red cubes lie in “hidden” positions the number of red–visible faces is 0; if one is hidden and one is on a face, then only 1 face shows red, etc.)

A key observation is that only cubes on the surface (i.e. not the single “interior” cube) can contribute to a red–visible face. (The only cube with no visible face is the center of the big cube.) Thus both red cubes must be among the 26 surface cubes.

On the surface the unit cubes fall into three types:
 • Corners – cubes at a vertex of the big cube. Each corner cube touches 3 faces. There are 8 corners.
 • Edges – cubes on an edge but not at a vertex. Each edge cube touches 2 faces. There are 12 edges.
 • Face–centers – cubes in the middle of a face. Each such cube touches 1 face. There are 6 face–centers.

When a red cube is placed in a given position it “contributes” its set of visible faces. (For example, a corner cube “contributes” 3 faces, an edge cube 2, and a face–center 1.) If the two red cubes lie in positions A and B with A “visible on” f(A) faces and B on f(B) faces, and if they share some faces then the total number of distinct faces showing red is
  |f(A) ∪ f(B)| = f(A) + f(B) – |f(A) ∩ f(B)|.
We want this union to have exactly 4 faces.

Thus, if we denote by f the number of faces a cube “touches” and by i the number of faces in common between the two red cubes, we must have
  f(A) + f(B) – i = 4.

Since f(A) and f(B) can be 3, 2, or 1 (and note that interior cubes with f = 0 are not allowed) we now break the possibilities into cases according to the types of positions chosen for the two red cubes. (Remember that the red cubes are “labeled” only by their positions; they are identical but the positions are distinct.)

──────────────────────────────
Case 1. Both red cubes are in corner positions.
 • Each corner has f = 3.
 • Then the union size is 3 + 3 – i = 6 – i.
 • To have 6 – i = 4 we must have i = 2.
When do two different corner cubes share exactly 2 faces? They do so exactly when they lie on a common edge of the big cube (since an edge is the intersection of 2 faces). And every edge of the cube has exactly 2 corner cubes. Since there are 12 edges, there are 12 unordered pairs of corners that share an edge.
  Count for Case 1 = 12.

──────────────────────────────
Case 2. One red cube is a corner and the other is on an edge.
 • The corner gives f = 3 and the edge gives f = 2.
 • Their union is 3 + 2 – i = 5 – i.
 • For 5 – i = 4 we need i = 1.
Now, when does a corner and an edge cube share exactly 1 face? Think of a given corner cube v. It touches 3 faces. An edge cube lies on 2 faces. For the two cubes to share exactly one face the edge cube must lie on one of the 3 faces that v touches but not on both of the two faces that meet at v. (If the edge cube lay on an edge incident to v then it would share 2 faces.)
On any given face that v touches there are 4 edge cubes. Two of these lie on the two edges through v (and would yield i = 2), while the other 2 lie on the opposite two edges of that face and so share exactly 1 face with v.
Thus for each corner there are 3 faces × 2 = 6 edge cubes that yield i = 1.
Since there are 8 corners, the total number of (corner, edge) pairs is 8 × 6 = 48.
  Count for Case 2 = 48.

──────────────────────────────
Case 3. One red cube is a corner and the other is a face–center.
 • The corner has f = 3 and the face–center has f = 1.
 • Their union is 3 + 1 – i = 4 – i.
 • To have 4 – i = 4 we need i = 0.
That is, the corner and the face–center must lie on no common face. A corner touches 3 faces, so the face–center must lie on one of the 3 faces not touched by that corner.
For each corner there are exactly 3 face–centers (one per “opposite” face) that do not share a face with it.
With 8 corners this gives 8 × 3 = 24 pairs.
  Count for Case 3 = 24.

──────────────────────────────
Case 4. Both red cubes are on edges.
 • Each edge cube has f = 2.
 • Then the union is 2 + 2 – i = 4 – i.
 • To have 4 – i = 4 we need i = 0.
That is, the two edge cubes must lie on disjoint sets of faces (i.e. they do not lie on a common face).
It is convenient to “label” an edge cube by the pair of faces on which it lies. (For example, an edge cube on the intersection of the left face and the front face is labeled {left, front}.) There are 12 such edges (one for each edge of the big cube). Two edge cubes share a face exactly when their two–element sets intersect.
We now want to count the number of unordered pairs of distinct edges whose corresponding face–pairs are disjoint.
A short counting argument shows that each edge has 5 other edges whose face–pairs are disjoint and that in all there are (12×5)/2 = 30 such pairs.
  Count for Case 4 = 30.

──────────────────────────────
The other type combinations (for example, one red cube on an edge and one on a face–center, or both on face–centers) would yield unions of size 3 or less and so are not allowed.

──────────────────────────────
Now, adding the counts from the four cases we get:
  Total = 12 + 48 + 24 + 30 = 114.

Thus, there are 114 ways to choose positions for the 2 red cubes (with the remaining 25 white cubes filling the other positions) so that exactly 4 faces of the 3×3×3 cube show red.

Answer: 114.
